name: Ghost surgery

card.summary: Undisclosed substitution of the operating surgeon, relevant to anyone choosing a cosmetic surgeon because of that surgeon's results and reputation.
card.note: Documented cases include deaths after cosmetic procedures in South Korea; consent rules and operating-room recording laws vary by country.

quick.overview:
Ghost surgery is when a surgeon other than the one the patient chose and consented to performs some or all of an operation, usually while the patient is under anesthesia and without being told. For people pursuing cosmetic surgery, it matters because the surgeon's skill and portfolio are the reason they were chosen, and the final look depends on who actually operates [2][3].

The practice is documented in medical ethics and law literature, and in South Korea it became a public issue in the 2010s after deaths in plastic surgery clinics. Professional bodies treat it as a breach of informed consent, and courts have treated it as battery in some jurisdictions [1][2][5].
quick.how: It is not a method anyone adopts to look better; it is a risk patients meet when selecting surgeons. Patient-safety discussions describe asking in advance who will perform each part of the operation and getting that role written into the consent form, and in Korea operating-room cameras are now required by law [2][3].
quick.risks: Reported harms include complications from less experienced operators, billing under the wrong name, and in documented Korean cases death from bleeding after jaw surgery [2]. Legal consequences for surgeons have included malpractice damages and, in one Korean case, a prison sentence [2].

lead: Ghost surgery is an operation performed by a substitute surgeon in place of the one who was hired and credited, usually after the patient is anesthetized. The American College of Surgeons defines it as surgery where the patient is not informed of, or is misled about, the identity of the operating surgeon [2][3].

It is relevant to appearance because cosmetic patients commonly choose a surgeon by before-and-after results and reputation. When a different person operates, the outcome reflects that person's skill rather than the surgeon whose work the patient viewed [2].
The practice has been discussed in medical journals since at least the 1970s, in ethics, legal and nursing literature, and has been the subject of legislation in South Korea [4][5][6].

chain: Patient picks a surgeon based on results
Result depends on an unchosen operator's skill
angle.text: Ghost surgery is a risk faced by cosmetic surgery patients, not a technique. Patient-safety guidance describes confirming who will operate, because the aesthetic outcome depends on the operator [2][4].

paras: The term originally described qualified surgeons operating in place of unqualified credited physicians, and by the late 1970s, after publicized cases involving a medical equipment salesman, it came to cover any case where someone other than the credited surgeon operates [2]. Nursing and surgical journals extend it to assistants, residents, physician assistants or partner surgeons who operate without the patient's knowledge [8].
Disclosed teaching arrangements, where patients are told residents may take part under supervision, are treated as different from ghost surgery [2][8].

A 1978 report commissioned by the New York Assembly Speaker found that residents performed 50 to 95 percent of operations in teaching hospitals, concluding care quality was generally not reduced but patients were not properly informed [2]. In a 1975 New York case, a prosthetics salesman took part in a hip operation and records were altered; the patient later settled a malpractice suit [2].

In South Korea the practice grew in the 2010s with the plastic surgery and medical tourism boom, allowing surgeons to double-book patients; the Korean Society of Plastic Surgeons estimated about 100,000 affected patients from 2008 to 2014 [2]. In October 2016 a student, Kwon Dae-hee, died of bleeding after jaw surgery largely performed by a general doctor and unsupervised assistants; the surgeon was sentenced in 2021 to three years for involuntary manslaughter [2].

The American Medical Association's ethics opinions and the American College of Surgeons treat undisclosed substitution as a violation of informed consent [1][3]. Legal analyses describe battery, fraud and malpractice claims, and a US federal case allowed several causes of action [5][7]. A study of Korean law noted the Medical Service Act addresses informed consent but lacked penalties for ghost surgery itself [9].

In August 2021 South Korea passed the Kwon Dae-hee bill requiring cameras in operating rooms; hospitals and the Korean Medical Association opposed it, citing privacy, while a survey cited in coverage found 97.9 percent public support [2].
No studies found. Related research includes a 2025 systematic review of remote proctoring in robotic surgery, which covers supervised mentoring and not covert substitution [10].

timeline.event: A New York Times report covers a hospital unit barring ghost surgeons [2].
New York report finds residents perform most teaching-hospital operations and patients are poorly informed [2].
Death of Kwon Dae-hee in South Korea after jaw surgery [2].
South Korea passes the operating-room camera law [2].
